questions.question: Describe how shack fires and floods destroy housing in South Africa, with examples, and state what people displaced by each need from an emergency shelter.
questions.expected_answer: Shack fires start when a paraffin stove, candle or illegal electrical connection ignites a home built of timber, hardboard, cardboard, plastic and iron; with shacks a metre apart and no fire breaks, radiant heat and wind carry the fire faster than people can wake, as in Imizamo Yethu in 2017 where over two thousand homes were lost and about ten thousand people displaced in a night, leaving a field of ash and iron sheets and people escaping with what they wear, often without documents or food. They need a dry, warm, safe place to sleep that same night, for hundreds at once, on debris-covered ground, with fire spacing. Floods come from heavy rain, overflowing rivers and blocked or absent storm drains; in April 2022 more than 300 millimetres fell on parts of KwaZulu-Natal in a day, rivers rose metres in hours, shacks were washed off slopes, roads and bridges collapsed, more than four hundred people died and thousands lost homes. Belongings are soaked, roads are cut so help is slow, water is contaminated and the ground is mud, so the shelter must have a raised or waterproof floor, stand on soft soil in wind and last weeks while homes are repaired or relocated.

questions.question: Describe how earthquakes and political strife create the need for shelters, with South African examples, and set out the brief that all four scenarios share and the details that differ.
questions.expected_answer: In August 2014 a magnitude 5.5 earthquake near Orkney damaged hundreds of houses in Khuma and surrounding townships and was felt across the region; after a quake, aftershocks and unstable walls mean people cannot re-enter even intact-looking homes until they are checked, so they sleep outside for days beside their possessions, and shelters must go up quickly on open ground and be light enough to cause no harm if knocked down. In May 2008 xenophobic violence killed more than sixty people and drove tens of thousands of foreign nationals to police stations, churches and halls, some for months, with recurrences in 2015; strife makes people flee suddenly and far, afraid to return, at risk of being targeted again, often without local language or documents, so shelters must give safety and privacy, may be set up beside existing buildings and may be needed long term. The shared brief is a shelter within hours, for families with privacy and a door, sturdy in wind, waterproof, floored against wet or sharp ground, erectable by the occupants with few tools, light to transport and move, lasting at least a month and safe from the stoves that will be used inside. Details differ: raised floors for floods, lightness for earthquakes, separation and lockable doors for strife, and fire spacing for a settlement that has burned.

questions.question: Explain, with examples, how technology is both a cause and a cure in these disasters, and describe the social and environmental impacts a shelter designer must weigh.
questions.expected_answer: As a cause: the cheap paraffin stove and illegal electrical connections start shack fires; dense settlement layouts without fire breaks spread them; hard surfaces, drains blocked by plastic waste, housing on flood plains and steep slopes and heavier rain from a changing climate worsen floods; deep mining sets off tremors; social media spreads rumours that spark xenophobic violence. As a cure: shelters from plastic sheet to tent to prefabricated unit; phone flood alerts that saved lives in 2022; fire pumps and water tankers; purification tablets and mobile toilets; registration databases that help families prove identity and reunite; temporary classrooms; wide-based safer stoves and solar lamps; and networked community smoke alarms in Cape Town settlements. Impacts to weigh: abandoned plastic shelters become waste; imported tents cost foreign money and arrive late while locally made shelters from local materials arrive sooner and give local work; shelters that are too permanent become unplanned settlements, as after 2008; shelters that are too flimsy fail in the first storm and displace families twice. An answer names the technology, who it helps and how, who or what it harms, and how the design could keep the benefit and reduce the harm.
